ed2a1be0-cab3-4e3b-8b08-411b5f05c261.recap: Andy Constant of Damped Spring Advisors lays out a four-factor macro framework (growth, inflation, risk premium, positioning) and argues growth expectations are now too high across every asset class after a sharp bond sell-off finally repriced rates alongside already-strong equities. His central worry is a mismatch between AI-driven earnings claims from mega-cap companies and total US GDP ("the pie theory"), plus the scale of debt-financed AI capex ("hamburger theory") that could strain financing markets. He notes six prior COVID-era episodes where rapid 50-125bp rate spikes V-topped as policymakers intervened, and questions whether a seventh V-top is coming; Treasury Secretary Bessent's expanded buybacks and reported mortgage purchases by Pulte are read as administration attempts to suppress long-end yields ahead of the November refunding. On the Fed, he's skeptical Kevin Warsh has yet proven credibility — the September hike was forced by data, not a voluntary hawkish signal — and doubts, based on the post-Volcker track record, that any Fed will actually inflict enough pain (higher rates, lower asset prices, job losses) to bring demand-driven inflation to target. He argues this cycle's leverage is unusually public-sector (national debt) rather than private-sector driven, making historical analogs weak. His own book: roughly 75% of a 4%-worst-case risk budget, short equities, long long-duration bonds, small long JPY, and a small long SOFR position, framed as a 1-3 month tactical overlay atop a permanent, levered risk-parity-style beta portfolio (bonds/stocks/commodities/gold).
terms: SOFR -- Secured Overnight Financing Rate, the US repo-based benchmark for short-term interest rates
V-top -- a rapid spike in interest rates that quickly reverses, as speaker uses it for repeated post-COVID rate episodes
60/40 -- a traditional portfolio allocation of 60% equities and 40% bonds
zero DTE options -- options contracts with zero days to expiration
